goals: Explain system, surroundings and the types of system, and the idea of a state function
Define internal energy, heat and work and apply the first law ΔU = q + w
Calculate pressure–volume work, relate ΔH to ΔU, and use heat capacity and calorimetry
Find reaction enthalpies with standard enthalpies of formation and Hess's law; recognise the different kinds of enthalpy
Understand entropy, the second and third laws, and use Gibbs energy to judge spontaneity and equilibrium (ΔG° = −RT ln K)

system.def: The part of the universe chosen for study.

surroundings.def: Everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it.

open.def: A system that exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings.

closed.def: A system that exchanges energy but not matter.

isolated.def: A system that exchanges neither matter nor energy.

statefn.def: A property whose value depends only on the present state, not on the path taken (e.g. U, H, S, G).

extensive.def: A property that depends on the amount of matter (mass, volume, U, H).

intensive.def: A property independent of the amount of matter (temperature, pressure, density).

internal-energy.def: The total energy contained in the system (chemical, electrical, mechanical, …); symbol U.

work.def: A mode of energy transfer between system and surroundings (w); a path-dependent quantity.

heat.def: Energy transferred because of a temperature difference (q).

adiabatic.def: A process in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (q = 0).

first-law.def: ΔU = q + w; energy can be neither created nor destroyed.

isothermal.def: A process carried out at constant temperature (ΔT = 0).

reversible.def: A process carried out infinitely slowly, always near equilibrium, that a tiny change can reverse.

irreversible.def: An ordinary, finite-rate process that takes place away from equilibrium.

enthalpy.def: H = U + pV; at constant pressure the heat absorbed or released equals ΔH.

heat-capacity.def: Heat needed to raise the temperature by 1 K (C = q/ΔT).

specific-heat.def: Heat needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K).

calorimeter.def: An apparatus used to measure heat changes of reactions.

std-state.def: The pure form of a substance at 1 bar and the stated temperature.

formation.def: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their reference states (ΔfH°).

thermochem.def: A balanced equation written with ΔH and the physical states of the substances.

hess.en: Hess's law of constant heat summation
hess.def: The total enthalpy change is the same whether a reaction takes place in one step or in several.

combustion.def: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen (ΔcH°).

atomization.def: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance is converted to gaseous atoms (ΔaH°).

bond-enthalpy.def: Enthalpy needed to break 1 mol of a bond in the gas phase.

lattice.def: Enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid is separated into gaseous ions.

born-haber.def: An enthalpy cycle using Hess's law to find lattice enthalpy.

spontaneous.def: A process that can occur on its own without outside help.

entropy.def: A measure of the disorder of a system (S); a state function.

second-law.def: In a spontaneous process the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) increases.

third-law.def: The entropy of a perfectly crystalline pure substance is zero at absolute zero.

gibbs.def: G = H − TS; the criterion of spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure.

blocks.text: In a chemical reaction energy changes hands: heat may be released or absorbed. Thermodynamics keeps the books on these energy changes and tells us whether a reaction can occur and how far it can go. It cannot tell us how fast it will happen.

First, a few terms. The part of the universe we study is the [[system]]; everything else is the [[surroundings]]. The real or imaginary surface between them is the boundary. So universe = system + surroundings.
Depending on what can cross the boundary, a system is one of three kinds:

items: [[open]] — both matter and energy are exchanged. Example: hot water in an open beaker.
[[closed]] — only energy is exchanged, not matter. Example: water in a sealed conducting vessel.
[[isolated]] — neither matter nor energy is exchanged. Example: an ideal thermos flask.

blocks.name: thermo-system
blocks.title: Types of system
blocks.caption: Pick a system type and try to push matter and heat across the boundary — what does it let through?

blocks.text: The state of a system is described by its pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T), amount (n) and so on. Such quantities are [[statefn]]s (state variables): their values depend only on the present state, not on how the system got there. When the state changes, the change in a state function depends only on the initial and final states.
In thermodynamics we look only at the initial and final states; the path in between does not matter for a state function.

sections.title: Internal energy and the first law

blocks.text: All the energy held inside a system — chemical, electrical, mechanical and so on — is its [[internal-energy]] (U). We cannot find the absolute value of U, but we can measure its change ΔU. U can change in three ways: by heat exchange, by work, and by exchange of matter.

First take an adiabatic system, in which no heat can enter or leave (q = 0). Joule's experiments showed that the same amount of adiabatic work takes a system between the same two states, however the work is done. So ΔU = w(adiabatic), and U is a state function.

In general a system exchanges both [[heat]] (q) and [[work]] (w). With the IUPAC sign convention q is positive when the system absorbs heat and w is positive when work is done on the system. Heat released by the system, or work done by the system, is negative.

blocks.label: First law
blocks.text: ΔU = q + w

This is the [[first-law]]: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted. For an isolated system q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔU = 0. Note that q and w individually depend on the path, but their sum q + w = ΔU does not.

blocks.name: thermo-firstlaw
blocks.title: ΔU = q + w
blocks.caption: Change q and w and watch ΔU. Book Example 5.7 (701 J absorbed, 394 J of work done by the gas) is preloaded.

blocks.text: Example (book 5.7): a system absorbing 701 J of heat and doing 394 J of work has ΔU = +701 + (−394) = +307 J. In an adiabatic case ΔU = w; at constant volume ΔU = q.

When a reaction produces or uses a gas, pressure–volume work is usually done. Picture a gas under a piston; if the external pressure is p_{ex} and the volume changes from V_{i} to V_{f}, the work done on the system is:

blocks.label: Pressure–volume work
blocks.text: w = −p_{ex}ΔV = −p_{ex}(V_{f} − V_{i})
In expansion V_{f} > V_{i}, so w is negative — the system does work; in compression w is positive. On a p–V diagram the work is the area under the line of the external pressure.

In a [[reversible]] process the external and internal pressures differ only infinitesimally (p_{ex} = p ± dp) and w = −∫p dV. In an [[irreversible]] process this is not so. For the isothermal reversible expansion of n mol of an ideal gas:

blocks.label: Isothermal reversible work
blocks.text: w_{rev} = −nRT ln(V_{f}/V_{i}) = −2.303 nRT log(V_{f}/V_{i})

blocks.name: thermo-pvwork
blocks.title: p–V work: reversible versus irreversible
blocks.caption: 1 mol of ideal gas expands from 2 L. The shaded area is the work done; the reversible path gives the maximum work.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas ΔU = 0 in an isothermal expansion (Joule), so q = −w. In a free expansion into vacuum (p_{ex} = 0), w = 0 and q = 0. In book Example 5.3, expansion from 2 L to 10 L against 1 atm gives w = −1 × 8 = −8 L atm. (Book Example 5.4 prints R as 0.8206; the correct value is 0.08206 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, giving |w| ≈ 39.4 L atm for 1 mol expanding reversibly from 2 to 10 L at 298 K.)

At constant volume (ΔV = 0), w = 0 and so ΔU = q_{V}. But most reactions run in open vessels, i.e. at constant pressure, where ΔU = q_{p} − pΔV, so q_{p} = ΔU + pΔV. This combination defines a new state function, [[enthalpy]]:

blocks.label: Enthalpy
blocks.text: H = U + pV      ΔH = ΔU + pΔV = q_{p}

In an exothermic reaction ΔH is negative; in an endothermic reaction it is positive. Solids and liquids change volume very little, so ΔH and ΔU differ appreciably only when the number of moles of gas changes:

blocks.label: ΔH and ΔU
blocks.text: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_{g}RT

Here Δn_{g} = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants). Example 5.5: for 1 mol H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at 373 K, ΔH = 41.00 kJ mol⁻¹, so ΔU = 41.00 − (1)(8.314 × 10⁻³)(373) = 37.904 kJ mol⁻¹.

Properties that depend on the amount of matter are [[extensive]] (mass, volume, U, H, heat capacity); those that do not are [[intensive]] (temperature, pressure, density). Cut a vessel into two equal halves: V and n halve, but T and p stay the same. The ratio of two extensive properties (such as molar volume V/n) is intensive.

When a substance absorbs heat its temperature rises: q = C × ΔT, where C is the [[heat-capacity]]. For 1 mol it is the molar heat capacity (C_{m}); for 1 g it is the [[specific-heat]] (c), and q = c × m × ΔT. Water has a large heat capacity, so it takes a lot of heat to warm it.
At constant volume q_{V} = C_{V}ΔT = ΔU; at constant pressure q_{p} = C_{p}ΔT = ΔH. For 1 mol of ideal gas ΔH = ΔU + RΔT, hence:

The energy change of a reaction is measured in a [[calorimeter]]. To find ΔU **at constant volume** a bomb calorimeter is used: the sample and oxygen are sealed in a steel bomb, immersed in water and ignited electrically, and the temperature rise is read. Since ΔV = 0, w = 0 and q_{V} = ΔU. Heat measured **at constant pressure** (an open vessel) is q_{p} = ΔH. If the calorimeter's heat capacity C is known, q = C × ΔT.

blocks.name: thermo-calorimeter
blocks.title: Bomb calorimeter and ΔH versus ΔU
blocks.caption: In the first view change C and ΔT to obtain ΔU; in the second view see the effect of Δn_{g}RT.

blocks.text: Example 5.6 (book): 1 g of graphite burns in a bomb calorimeter at 298 K and the temperature rises from 298 K to 299 K; C = 20.7 kJ K⁻¹. So ΔU = −20.7 kJ g⁻¹ = −(20.7 × 12.0) = −2.48 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹; as Δn_{g} = 0, ΔH = ΔU.
In a reaction the reactants turn into products. The enthalpy change that goes with this is the reaction enthalpy Δ_{r}H:

blocks.label: Reaction enthalpy
blocks.text: Δ_{r}H = Σ a_{i}H(products) − Σ b_{i}H(reactants)

Because reaction enthalpy depends on conditions, the [[std-state]] is fixed: the pure form of a substance at 1 bar and the stated temperature (usually 298 K). The standard state of liquid water at 298 K is pure liquid water at 1 bar. The ° sign on Δ_{r}H° marks standard conditions.

Changes of state also involve enthalpy: melting ice needs Δ_{fus}H° = 6.00 kJ mol⁻¹ (273 K) and vaporising water needs Δ_{vap}H° = 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹ (373 K). The reverse process has the opposite sign. A solid turning directly to vapour has Δ_{sub}H° (for CO₂ 25.2 kJ mol⁻¹ at 195 K).

The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their reference states is the [[formation]] (Δ_{f}H°). An element's reference state is its most stable form at 298 K and 1 bar, so Δ_{f}H° = 0 for such elements (H₂(g), O₂(g), C(graphite), Br₂(l), …).
The standard enthalpy of any reaction can be found from such data:

blocks.label: Δ_{r}H° from Δ_{f}H°
blocks.text: Δ_{r}H° = Σ a_{i}Δ_{f}H°(products) − Σ b_{i}Δ_{f}H°(reactants)

blocks.name: thermo-enthalpy
blocks.title: Enthalpy diagram and Δ_{f}H° bookkeeping
blocks.caption: Pick a reaction; the diagram shows the reactant and product levels measured from the elements (zero line) and the resulting ΔᵣH°.

blocks.text: Example: for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3H₂(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O(l), Δ_{r}H° = 3(−285.83) − (−824.2) = −33.3 kJ mol⁻¹. For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), Δ_{r}H° = (−635.09) + (−393.51) − (−1206.92) = +178.3 kJ mol⁻¹ — limestone absorbs heat as it decomposes.

**[[thermochem]]:** a balanced equation is written together with ΔH and the physical states (s, l, g, aq). Rules: (1) coefficients mean moles, so doubling the equation doubles ΔH; (2) reversing the equation changes the sign of ΔH; (3) always state the physical states. E.g. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g); Δ_{r}H° = −91.8 kJ mol⁻¹, and the reverse reaction has ΔH = +91.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

**[[hess]]:** ΔH is a state function, so the total ΔH is the same whether the reaction takes one step or several. Just add the step enthalpies (Δ_{r}H = Δ_{r}H₁ + Δ_{r}H₂ + Δ_{r}H₃ + …). For instance, C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO cannot be measured directly because CO₂ also forms:

blocks.label: Hess's law example
blocks.text:
(i)  C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂;   Δ_{r}H° = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹
(ii) CO + ½O₂ → CO₂;   Δ_{r}H° = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹
(i) − (ii):  C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO;   Δ_{r}H° = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.name: thermo-hess
blocks.title: Hess's law: adding the steps
blocks.caption: Add the steps one at a time and watch the total ΔH build up.

sections.title: Enthalpies for different types of reactions

blocks.text: **[[combustion]] (Δ_{c}H°):** the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen. Combustion is exothermic, so Δ_{c}H° is always negative. Example: C₄H₁₀(g) + 13/2 O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l); Δ_{c}H° = −2658.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Burning glucose gives Δ_{c}H° = −2802.0 kJ mol⁻¹ — breaking down food in our body releases the same energy.
Book Example 5.9: burning 1 mol C₆H₆(l) releases 3267.0 kJ; with Δ_{f}H° of CO₂ and H₂O(l) equal to −393.5 and −285.83 kJ mol⁻¹, Δ_{f}H°(C₆H₆) = 6(−393.5) + 3(−285.83) + 3267.0 = +48.51 kJ mol⁻¹.

**[[atomization]] (Δ_{a}H°):** the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance is converted to gaseous atoms. H₂(g) → 2H(g); Δ_{a}H° = 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹. CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g); Δ_{a}H° = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. For a metal it equals the sublimation enthalpy: Na(s) → Na(g); Δ_{a}H° = 108.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

**[[bond-enthalpy]] (Δ_{bond}H°):** in diatomic molecules (H₂, Cl₂, O₂) the bond dissociation enthalpy equals the atomisation enthalpy (H–H = 435.0, Cl–Cl = 242 kJ mol⁻¹). In polyatomic molecules such as CH₄ the four C–H bonds need different energies: 427, 439, 452 and 347 kJ mol⁻¹, totalling 1665. So the mean C–H bond enthalpy = 1665 ÷ 4 ≈ 416 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.label: ΔH from bond enthalpies
blocks.text: Δ_{r}H° = Σ (bond enthalpies of reactants) − Σ (bond enthalpies of products)
This works best for substances in the gas phase and gives only approximate values (mean bond enthalpies are used). Breaking bonds costs energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases it (exothermic).

**[[lattice]] (Δ_{lattice}H°):** the enthalpy needed to separate 1 mol of an ionic solid into gaseous ions; NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g); Δ_{lattice}H° = +788 kJ mol⁻¹. It cannot be measured directly, so the [[born-haber]] is used: applying Hess's law to sublimation (+108.4), ionisation (+496), half the Cl–Cl dissociation (+121), electron gain (−348.6) and formation (−411.2) gives lattice enthalpy = 411.2 + 108.4 + 121 + 496 − 348.6 = 788 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.name: thermo-cycle
blocks.title: Born–Haber cycle, enthalpy of solution and bond enthalpy
blocks.caption: Choose one of three examples and add its steps one at a time.

blocks.text: **Enthalpy of solution (Δ_{sol}H°)** is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance dissolves in a stated amount of solvent. For an ionic compound Δ_{sol}H° = Δ_{lattice}H° + Δ_{hyd}H°; for NaCl, 788 − 784 = +4 kJ mol⁻¹. **Enthalpy of dilution** is the enthalpy change on diluting a solution; e.g. dissolving HCl(g) in 10, 25, 40 and ∞ mol of water gives ΔH = −69.01, −72.3, −72.79 and −74.85 kJ mol⁻¹.

The first law says the energy books must balance but not which change will happen on its own. Everyday experience: hot objects cool down by themselves, a gas spreads into a vacuum, water flows downhill. A change that occurs without outside help is [[spontaneous]]. A spontaneous process is always irreversible, and can be reversed only with help from an external agency.

**Is a fall in enthalpy the criterion?** Many spontaneous reactions are exothermic — ½N₂ + 3/2 H₂ → NH₃ (ΔH = −46 kJ mol⁻¹), H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l) (ΔH = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹). But ½N₂ + O₂ → NO₂ (ΔH = +33.2 kJ mol⁻¹) and C(graphite) + 2S(s) → CS₂(l) (ΔH = +128.5 kJ mol⁻¹) are endothermic yet occur; ice melts (endothermic) and a gas spreads into vacuum (ΔH = 0). So a fall in enthalpy alone is not the full criterion.

**[[entropy]] and spontaneity:** when a gas spreads into a vacuum ΔH = 0 and yet the change occurs — because the arrangement of the particles becomes more disordered. The measure of disorder is the entropy S: the more disordered the system, the larger S. A liquid has more entropy than a solid, a gas more than a liquid; raising the temperature also raises entropy because the particles move more. For a reversible process ΔS = q_{rev}/T.

blocks.name: thermo-entropy
blocks.title: Entropy: particles spreading
blocks.caption: Remove the partition and watch the particles spread. The chance of them all returning to one side is tiny.

blocks.text: **[[second-law]]:** in a spontaneous process the total entropy of the system plus surroundings increases:

blocks.label: Second law
blocks.text: ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{sys} + ΔS_{surr} > 0      ΔS_{surr} = −ΔH_{sys}/T (constant p)

Example 5.11 (book): for 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ at 298 K, ΔS_{sys} = −549.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −1648 × 10³ J mol⁻¹. ΔS_{surr} = 1648 × 10³/298 = +5530 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so ΔS_{total} = 5530 − 549.4 ≈ +4980.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ > 0 — the reaction is spontaneous (iron rusts).

**Absolute entropy and the [[third-law]]:** cooling reduces the motion of the particles and so the entropy. At absolute zero (0 K) the entropy of a pure, perfectly crystalline substance is zero. This lets us find absolute entropies by measuring ∫(C_{p}/T)dT from 0 K up to T.
Applying the second law requires ΔS of the surroundings, which is awkward. To decide spontaneity from properties of the system alone we define a new state function, the [[gibbs]] (G):

blocks.label: Gibbs equation
blocks.text: G = H − TS      at constant T and p: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
From ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{sys} − ΔH_{sys}/T we get ΔG = −TΔS_{total}. In a spontaneous process ΔS_{total} > 0, so:

items: ΔG < 0 — the process is spontaneous (and useful work can be obtained);
ΔG > 0 — the process is not spontaneous (the reverse is);
ΔG = 0 — the system is at equilibrium.

blocks.text: ΔG is a contest between ΔH and TΔS. If ΔH is negative (exothermic) and ΔS positive, ΔG < 0 always. If they have the same sign, temperature decides; the crossover temperature is T = ΔH/ΔS. Book Table 5.4:

blocks.name: thermo-gibbs
blocks.title: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: the spontaneity map
blocks.caption: Vary ΔH, ΔS and T; the line shows ΔG and the crossover temperature where it passes through zero.

blocks.text: **Equilibrium:** at equilibrium the reaction goes both ways at equal rates, so ΔG = 0. For reactants and products in their standard states, the standard Gibbs energy change (Δ_{r}G°) is related to the equilibrium constant K by:

blocks.label: Δ_{r}G° and K
blocks.text: Δ_{r}G° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K      (Δ_{r}G° = Δ_{r}H° − TΔ_{r}S°)

If Δ_{r}G° is negative, K > 1 and products dominate; if positive, K < 1 and reactants dominate. Knowing Δ_{r}G° gives K, and vice versa. Book Example 5.12: for 3/2 O₂ → O₃ with K_{p} = 2.47 × 10⁻²⁹, Δ_{r}G° = −2.303(8.314)(298) log(2.47 × 10⁻²⁹) ≈ +163 kJ mol⁻¹. Example 5.13: for Δ_{r}G° = −13.6 kJ mol⁻¹, log K = 13600/(2.303 × 8.314 × 298) = 2.38, so K ≈ 2.4 × 10².

blocks.name: thermo-gibbsk
blocks.title: Δ_{r}G° and the equilibrium constant K
blocks.caption: Change Δ_{r}G° and T and see K and the equilibrium composition.

summary: Thermodynamics tracks the energy changes of chemical and physical processes. Universe = system + surroundings; a system may be open, closed or isolated.
First law: ΔU = q + w; U is a state function while q and w depend on the path. In the IUPAC convention q > 0 when the system absorbs heat and w > 0 when work is done on it.
Pressure–volume work is w = −p_{ex}ΔV; for the isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas w = −2.303 nRT log(V_{f}/V_{i}) and ΔU = 0.
Enthalpy H = U + pV; q_{p} = ΔH at constant pressure, q_{V} = ΔU at constant volume, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_{g}RT; C_{p} − C_{V} = R.
In a calorimeter q = C × ΔT; a bomb calorimeter measures ΔU.
Δ_{r}H° = ΣΔ_{f}H°(products) − ΣΔ_{f}H°(reactants); Δ_{f}H° = 0 for elements in their reference states. Hess's law: the total ΔH is independent of the path.
Definitions of combustion, atomisation, bond, lattice, solution and dilution enthalpies; the Born–Haber cycle gives the lattice enthalpy of NaCl = +788 kJ mol⁻¹.
Entropy S measures disorder; ΔS_{total} > 0 for a spontaneous process (second law); S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K (third law).
Gibbs energy ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: ΔG < 0 spontaneous, ΔG = 0 equilibrium; Δ_{r}G° = −RT ln K.
